slides.notes: Second part of the lecture, in parallel with Assignment 9. Narrative: the hypermedia part showed how clients find their next action at run time, and that a shared conceptual model (RDF vocabularies) is the final step. Solid applies exactly these ideas to data at rest: pods are hypermedia over HTTP with RDF representations, and the owner of the data, not the application, controls access. We start with why (platforms and walled gardens), then the building blocks (pods, WebIDs, LDP, Solid-OIDC, WAC, type indexes, shapes, notifications), then PITAS and the critique, and end with the assignment and SoSy 27.

slides.title: Solid: Social Linked Data
points: Launched in 2016 by Tim Berners-Lee at MIT, to separate data from the apps that use it
Built from Web standards: HTTP, URIs, RDF, Linked Data Platform, OpenID Connect
Specified by the W3C Solid Community Group: the Solid Protocol (0.11) and companion specifications for identity, access control and notifications
Since 2024, the W3C Linked Web Storage Working Group turns it into a W3C standard
Servers: the open source Community Solid Server, which we use, and others

aside.alt: Solid logo: a white S in a purple hexagon

slides.notes: Solid stands for Social Linked Data (the name came from Sandro Hawke in the MIT and QCRI read-write linked data work). Inrupt was founded in 2018 as the company around Solid; the Open Data Institute is now the steward of the Solid project. The LWS Working Group was chartered on 9 September 2024; its charter lists the Solid Protocol 0.11.0 as input document.

slides.title: “…web applications where data storage, entity authentication, access control, and application provider are all loosely coupled”
slides.attribution: Mission of the W3C Linked Web Storage Working Group

Coupling again: the question of the last three lectures, now asked about data
slides.notes: Connect to lecture 7 and 8: we chose architectural constraints and interaction styles to control coupling between components. Solid moves the boundary: storage, identity, access control and application become four independently replaceable parts.

slides.title: Solid: Pods, WebIDs and Apps
slides.alt: Diagram: three applications (photo gallery, the PITAS app of group 3, a calendar) at the top, three pods at the bottom (Alice's pod with photos and calendar, an auction house pod with auctions and results, Bob's pod on his own server with photos and results); arrows show that each app reads and writes several pods, only with the owner's permission
slides.caption: A **pod** is a Web server space for one agent's data; a **WebID** is a URI that names an agent. Apps and pods are chosen independently.
slides.notes: Recall the personal data storage slides: separate markets for data and for services. Every pod has an owner identified by a WebID; one app can use many pods, one pod serves many apps. A pod can be hosted by a provider, by the institution, or on your own machine.

slides.title: WebID: A URI for Every Agent
points: The WebID `…/card#me` names the agent; the document `…/card` describes it
Dereferencing the WebID tells a client who vouches for the agent (`solid:oidcIssuer`), where its pod is (`pim:storage`) and where to look for its data (`solid:publicTypeIndex`)
An agent can be a person, an organisation or a piece of software: in PITAS, every participating entity
slides.caption: The profile is RDF in Turtle; relative URIs like `<../>` are resolved against the document.
slides.notes: Hash URI: the fragment #me separates the agent from the document about it (the person is not the document). The Community Solid Server creates this profile when you register; you add the type index link yourself (Assignment 9, Task 4.2).

                bids/             # append-only container
                    b-8f2c.ttl
        results/
points: Containers end with `/` and list their members with `ldp:contains`
Resources are RDF documents (Turtle, JSON-LD) or any other file: pictures, PDFs
Every resource has its own URI, so data in one pod can link to data in any other pod
slides.caption: One possible layout of an auction house's pod, from the Assignment 9 sheet. The task force decides the real one.
slides.notes: LDP = W3C Linked Data Platform 1.0 (2015). Solid uses LDP Basic Containers: the server maintains the ldp:contains triples. Point out that the URI structure is not a contract: clients should find containers by following links (type index, later), not by constructing paths.

slides.title: Reading and Writing Data: LDP over HTTP
rows: read the representation; a container lists its members
create a new resource in it; the server picks its URI (`Location`)
create or replace the resource at this URI
insert and delete triples with an N3 Patch
Append (only inserts), else Read and Write
slides.after: The methods of the uniform interface with their defined semantics. Solid adds RDF representations, identity and access control.
slides.notes: This is the REST uniform interface of lecture 7 and CRUD over HTTP from lecture 8, plus hypermedia: representations are RDF with links. Mention OPTIONS for discovering allowed methods (Allow, Accept-Post, Accept-Patch headers), and that the WAC-Allow header tells a client which modes it has. Live demo: curl against a local Community Solid Server (npx @solid/community-server), anonymous access to a public container.

slides.title: Example: Publishing an Auction
slides.code:
POST /pitas-g3/pitas/auctions/ HTTP/1.1
Host: solid.example.org
Authorization: DPoP eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIs…
DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIs…
Content-Type: text/turtle

@prefix pitas: <https://pitas.example.org/ns#> .
<#it> a pitas:Auction ;
  pitas:task <https://solid.example.org/c7/tasks/t-17.ttl> ;
  pitas:status pitas:Open .

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /pitas-g3/pitas/auctions/3f9a2c
points: `POST` to the container: the server mints the URI of the new resource and returns it in `Location`
The auction refers to the task in the client's pod by its URI: a link, not a copy
To choose the URI yourself, `PUT` to it, for example `…/auctions/a-001.ttl`
The two token headers say who is asking (Solid-OIDC, below)
slides.notes: The Solid Protocol no longer requires servers to honour the Slug header; the Community Solid Server does use it as a hint. The task URI points to another pod on possibly another server: this is the 'link to it from another pod' option of the sovereignty discussion.

slides.title: Changing Data: N3 Patch and ETags
points: `solid:where` is a condition: if the auction is no longer open, the server answers `409 Conflict`
`If-Match` sends the ETag of the version you read: if someone changed the document since, `412 Precondition Failed`
No transactions across resources: changing two documents takes two requests, and either can fail
slides.notes: Concurrency is now the pod's problem and the client's: there is no database transaction around an auction and its bids. This is the coupling that Assignment 9, Task 3.1, says will become visible (code that assumed transactional writes). Reflection question 1 asks about exactly this.

slides.title: Your Turn: Which Request?
items: A bidder submits a sealed bid for auction a-001. Which method, to which URI, with which access mode?
The auction house closes the auction, but only if it is still open. What does it send?
A client moves to another PITAS provider. What happens to its tasks?
Two PITAS apps read the same auction. What must they agree on?
slides.notes: Discuss in pairs for 3 minutes. Answers: POST to the bids container, Append; PATCH with solid:where (or If-Match); nothing, the tasks stay in the client's pod and the new provider gets access; HTTP, RDF and the shared vocabulary (next slides), not an API of each other.

slides.title: Who Is Asking? Solid-OIDC
slides.alt: Sequence diagram with four lifelines: PITAS app, identity provider, pod, WebID profile. 1 the app logs in as its WebID; 2 the identity provider returns a token that names the WebID, bound to the app's key with DPoP; 3 the app sends GET to the bids container with the token and a DPoP proof; 4 the pod dereferences the WebID and finds solid:oidcIssuer; 5 the pod checks the access rules; 6 it answers 200 OK, 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden
slides.caption: The pod trusts an identity provider only if the WebID profile names it. Your PITAS app logs in without a browser, with client credentials of the Community Solid Server.
slides.notes: Simplified: Solid-OIDC is OpenID Connect plus the webid claim plus DPoP (proof of possession): a stolen token is useless without the app's private key. Authentication (who is asking) is separated from authorization (what they may do), and both from the storage. Assignment 9, Task 4.1.

slides.title: Who May Do What? Web Access Control

callout.text: Why may bidders append to the bids container, but not write to it?

points: Modes: `Read`, `Write`, `Append` (add, never remove) and `Control` (change the rules)
`acl:accessTo` is the container itself, `acl:default` is inherited by everything in it
`acl:agent` names one WebID; `acl:agentClass foaf:Agent` is anyone
The pod enforces the sealed bid, not your code
slides.notes: Each resource links its ACL resource with Link: <…>; rel="acl". acl:AuthenticatedAgent is the class of all logged-in agents. ACP (Access Control Policy) is the alternative model with policies and matchers, used by Inrupt's server and optional in the Community Solid Server. Assignment 9, Task 4.3 asks for four rules; the sealed-bid one is shown here (as on the sheet).

slides.title: Finding Data: Follow Your Nose from the WebID
slides.alt: Chain of five boxes connected by arrows: WebID …/profile/card#me, profile document with solid:publicTypeIndex, public type index with solid:forClass pitas:Auction and solid:instanceContainer, container …/pitas/auctions/ with ldp:contains, auction a-001.ttl. Below: the bidder knows only the auction house's WebID; each step is a GET and a link to follow; the only shared knowledge is HTTP, RDF, the Solid vocabulary and the class pitas:Auction
slides.caption: Hypermedia for data at rest: this replaces the resource directory of Assignment 8 (Task 4.2). A private type index, readable only by the owner, lists private data.
slides.notes: Compare with HATEOAS: the client starts from one URI and follows typed links. The type index maps an RDF class to a container (solid:instanceContainer) or a single resource (solid:instance). This only works if all groups use the same class, which is the vocabulary question of the next slide.

slides.title: Data at Rest Needs a Contract: Vocabulary and Shapes
points: The API of Assignment 7 fixes messages in flight; pods hold data at rest that apps you never met will read
Reuse terms: schema.org for offers and prices, PROV-O for who produced what; mint `pitas:` terms only where nothing fits
A SHACL or ShEx shape lets an app validate data that it did not write
slides.caption: An example shape for a bid, not the one your task force will agree on.
slides.notes: Assignment 9, Task 2. The tension: the more precisely the task force specifies the data plane, the more interoperable the ecosystem and the less room each group has to evolve. Lecture 10 goes deeper into shared vocabularies and semantic interoperability.

slides.title: Pods Can Tell You: Solid Notifications

callout.text: Keep WebSub, or let the pods notify? (Assignment 9, Reflections)

points: A client subscribes to changes of a resource or a container, for example new bids
The pod lists its channels in its storage description, found through a `Link` header
`WebSocketChannel2023`: the client keeps a connection open; `WebhookChannel2023`: the pod calls the client back
In Assignment 8, a WebSub hub or an MQTT broker sat between publisher and subscriber
slides.notes: Solid decentralizes the data at rest; Assignment 8 decentralized the flow of events. With notifications, the pod becomes an event source too. The Community Solid Server supports WebSocket and Webhook channels. Ask: what does the hub give you that the pod does not (fan-out, retries, decoupling of publisher availability)?
slides.code:
POST /.notifications/WebSocketChannel2023/ HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/ld+json

{ "@context": [
    "https://www.w3.org/ns/solid/notifications-context/v1" ],
  "type": "WebSocketChannel2023",
  "topic": "…/pitas-g3/pitas/auctions/a-001/bids/" }

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

{ "type": "WebSocketChannel2023",
  "topic": "…/pitas-g3/pitas/auctions/a-001/bids/",
  "receiveFrom": "wss://solid.example.org/.notifications/…" }
slides.caption: Subscription to the bids container on a Community Solid Server.

slides.title: Data Sovereignty: Who Owns What?

callout.text: Whose pod does a bid belong in?

points: The sovereignty principle of Assignment 9: data stays in the pod of the entity that generates it, and only that entity decides who may use it
Others refer to it by its URI and keep no authoritative copies

sub: the auction is the house's record, but the task is the client's
a bid is the bidder's, but it is evidence for the house
a result is the worker's, but the client paid for it

slides.notes: Where ownership is contested, the group's role in the task force shapes the answer. Digital sovereignty: people, organisations and public institutions decide for themselves about their data and the infrastructure they depend on. The principle itself is fixed on the sheet; what it means for PITAS is Task 1. Note for the discussion: the example pod layout and ACL on the sheet put the bids into the auction house's pod, which is one possible answer to the callout question, not the only one.

slides.title: Solid in the PITAS Ecosystem
slides.alt: Diagram of PITAS under the sovereignty principle: on the course server solid.interactions.ics.unisg.ch the client's pod (tasks/t-17.ttl, WebID) and the auction house's pod (auctions/a-001.ttl, the bids container, WebID); on a group's own server the pod of a bidder and worker (bids/b-8f2c.ttl marked with a question mark, results/r-17.ttl, WebID). Dashed green links: the auction links to the task, the result links to the task. A red arrow labelled append? from the bidder to the bids container. Legend: pod of one entity, a link by URI and no copy, an open question for Task 1
slides.caption: The pod, not your application, is authoritative: stop your app, delete its local state, restart, and it continues from the pods (Task 3.1).
slides.notes: Walk through the sheet: which entities need a WebID and a pod, which data item lives where, which links and which permissions. The diagram is the kind of system diagram Task 1 asks for (with at least two other groups' applications). Pods spread over several servers must work: encourage a local Community Solid Server during development.

slides.title: Critical View: Where Does Solid Hurt?

callout.text: Which non-functional properties does Solid improve, and which does it cost?

points: Performance: following links means many small requests, across servers
Consistency: no transactions across resources and pods; partial failure is normal
Power: whoever hosts pods and identity providers gains a new central position
Usability: people must understand the access rules they set
Agreement: apps interoperate only if they share vocabularies and shapes
slides.notes: In the spirit of lectures 7 and 8: every architectural decision induces a non-functional profile. Solid improves evolvability, portability, autonomy of the data owner and privacy; it costs performance, simplicity and consistency. Prepare the task force discussion: what does a hyperscaler, a social media platform, a privacy activist and a government gain or lose? (Reflection question 5.)

slides.title: Any Questions / Comments / Doubts / Concerns?
points: Hypermedia lets clients find their next action at run time, as affordances do for people
Link relation types and media types tell a client why to follow a link and how to read the result
Solid separates data from apps: data lives in pods that its owners control
From a WebID, a client finds identity provider, storage and type index
Access rules live in the pod, not in each app's code
